new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexical (word) stress in Gaelic, and in the Colonsay dialect specifically, normally falls on the first syllable; the exception is compound words, where stress generally falls on the qualifying element (which may be the second element, e.g. bogha-frois [b̥oˈfrɔʃ], taigh-seinnse, or the first, e.g. meanbh-chuileagan). Lexical stress may be neutralised in connected speech when the word is not phrasally stressed. Stress conditions other prosodic features: glottalisation and clear preaspiration follow a short stressed vowel, and long vowels occur in principle only in stressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-internal secondary-stress rule is stated; secondary stress [ˌ] is mentioned only at phrase/compound level (e.g. subh craobh [ˌsu ˈkrø..v̥], càrn with secondary stress in a place-name, mòran with secondary stress in a sentence).
new_statements.exceptions: Compound words: stress generally on the qualifying element (bogha-frois [b̥oˈfrɔʃ], taigh-seinnse [təˈʃ[ɛi]ɲʃɪ] with non-initial stress vs meanbh-chuileagan with initial stress); place-name ceann tire (Kintyre) stressed on the second element (footnote, PDF the text); phrasal neutralisation of lexical stress in longer utterances.
new_statements.identity_note: Scouller 2018 describes the Scottish Gaelic dialect of the Inner Hebridean island of Colonsay (SGDS Point 57 and the author's own recordings), but explicitly says its stress behaviour does not differ substantially from other varieties of Gaelic.

tone_statements.quote: Lewis Gaelic distinguishes two tonal accent classes: Class 1 forms display an early pitch peak and Class 2 forms display a later pitch peak. The same contrast is realised in some other dialects by means of glottalisation or overlength. In ch. 4 I show that this contrast reflects syllable structure, and that the pitch peak occurs on the rightmost mora of the stressed syllable. … this tonal contrast can be analysed as reflecting not lexical tone but rather the alignment of intonational tonal autosegments with differing metrical structures in the phrase-level phonology.

tone_statements.summary: Lewis Gaelic: two tonal accents on the initial stressed syllable, pitch peak on its first vs second mora; analysed as intonational LH aligned to syllable weight, not lexical tone.

[...] A difference can also be heard in G[airloch] in the stress on the words, for there are two maxima of stress, equal or nearly so, on àth and on duan. But there is only one strong stress on adha and dubhan, heard in the first part of the vocalic segment, which carries the level tone.' -- p. 26: 'So, for the G[airloch] dialect, we are left where Oftedal was in Leurbost: no system of syllabic canons can be set up that fits the case; the distinction between words with hiatus vowels and words without hiatus vowels is easily and simply interpreted as one that depends on tone; but one is still reluctant (despite Borgstrøm 1974, Ternes 1980 and MacAulay 1992) to introduce phonemic tone into the phonology of the dialect.'

tone_statements.quote: p. 1: 'Most Gaelic varieties distinguish between: – Historical disyllables and svarabhakti words: balach ≠ balg – Historical long vowels/diphthongs and hiatus sequences: fitheach ≠ fiach • The contrast has long been recognized as akin to ‘tonal’ accent contrasts in North and West Germanic (Borgstrøm 1937, 1974, Macaulay 1993, Ternes 1980, 2006)'; p. 2: 'Lewis (Oftedal 1956, Ladefoged et al. 1998): – Accent 1 = rise-fall – Accent 2 = rise • Applecross (Ternes 2006) – Accent 1 = rise-fall, normal length in unstressed vowel – Accent 2 = ‘wavy contour’ (fall-rise-fall), overlength in unstressed vowel'; p. 11: 'Scottish Gaelic is not a ‘tonal language’ in the sense that we need no recourse to lexical tonal differences (‘contrastive tone’, following Ternes 2006) to derive the two accent classes'.
tone_statements.summary: Binary 'tonal accent' (accent 1 vs accent 2) across most Scottish Gaelic dialects, realised by pitch contour in Lewis/Wester Ross (rise-fall vs rise), by duration/overlength in Applecross, peak timing in Skye, glottalisation in Argyll; analysed metrically (foot structure), not as lexical tone.

tone_statements.quote: p. 93, as reproduced in Wentworth 2005: 24 (secondary; phonetic forms undecodable, shown /.; Wentworth's bracketed gloss omitted [...]): 'The dialect of Lewis has a peculiar pitch pattern : the pitch rises on a stressed syllable, particularly on the second half of it, and then falls again on following unstressed syllables. The pitch movement has a phonemic function in so far as it serves to distinguish monosyllables like bó “cow” /. or duan “poem” /. with rising pitch, from disyllables like bodha “sunken rock” /. or dubhan “fishing-hook” /. with rising-falling pitch. A pitch pattern closely resembling the Lewis one is used along the north and west coast of the Mainland down to Loch Torridon [...], i.e. in parts of Sutherland and Ross-shire. There is a striking resemblance between this pattern, particularly in its Lewis form, and toneme 1 “monosyllabic toneme” in South-Western Norwegian, e.g. in Stavanger.… Other Gaelic dialects, including all Hebridean dialects south of Lewis, present entirely different patterns usually with falling or level pitch on stressed syllables'.

tone_statements.summary: Lewis + NW mainland (Sutherland/Ross-shire coast to Loch Torridon): rising pitch on monosyllables (incl. long-vowel words) vs rising-falling on (hiatus) disyllables, explicitly called phonemic and compared to Norwegian toneme 1; contact (Norse) origin proposed.

tone_statements.quote: p. 89, as reproduced in Wentworth 2005: 16-17 (secondary; Borgstrøm's phonetic forms not decodable, shown as /.; a dropped pair of round brackets restored in square brackets): 'Intonation is an element of some importance ; it resembles the intonation used in Lewis. In Red P[oint] a stressed syllable has mainly rising tone ; often a slight fall is audible at the beginning of the syllable, but the end is always rising. An unaccented syllable has not as a rule rising tone [(]a slight rise may be heard in pausa[)] ; more often it is slightly falling and in any case lower than the end of the preceding stressed syllable. This change from rising to falling tone is the surest criterion of disyllabic pronunciation in words like /. “grandchild” ogha, /. “liver” atha, etc., where the second vowel is not separated from the first by a clear hiatus ; on the other hand words like /. “kiln” àith have rising tone to the end, and are thereby characterized as monosyllables'.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Wester Ross (Red Point/Gairloch): Lewis-like pitch pattern, rising on stressed syllables, falling/lower on unstressed; rising-then-falling contour marks (hiatus) disyllables vs rising-throughout monosyllables -- an impressionistic statement of the accent-1/accent-2 contrast realised by pitch, not framed as phonemic tone.

tone_statements.quote: All dialects of Gaelic reportedly have lexical stress on the first syllable in the word, and several dialects (including Lewis Gaelic) are said to have contrastive lexical pitch accents … According to previous descriptions, the lexical pitch accent contrast in Gaelic is based on syllabicity: pitch accented monosyllabic words have a rising or low pitch; and pitch accented polysyllabic words have a falling, high, or rising falling pitch … I refer to the monosyllabic Gaelic rise/low as Accent 1; and the more complex polysyllabic fall/rise-fall/high as Accent 2 (contra Ternes, 2006).
tone_statements.locator: p. 5, section 2 'Analysis 1: lexical pitch accent in Gaelic'; results p. 10-11 (sec. 2.3-2.4)
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical word accents (Swedish-type): Accent 1 rise/low on monosyllables, Accent 2 fall/rise-fall/high on polysyllables; low functional load; kept by older Lewis speakers, lost by the young.
